title: Reconciling, when safe
hook: where it's safe, reconciliation is a gift to both

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corinth, and your younger self. Your line was I didn't know then. Today, a step that takes two people, not one.

Two old friends pass in a grocery aisle. One hand goes halfway up, the other person nods, and both keep walking, carts rattling, each wondering if the other wanted to stop. A few weeks ago this path said forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship, and that's still true. But sometimes the distance isn't protecting anyone anymore. Sometimes the other person is safe, and sorry, or just as stuck. A Hebrew psalm and a Chinese classic each have a line about what happens when two people do stop.
screen: `A HALF-RAISED HAND.` → `FORGIVING CAN BE ALONE.` → `RECONCILING TAKES TWO.`

segments.voice: First, what it's for. Psalm 133 opens, in the King James words: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Not only right, but sweet to live in. The psalm compares it to fragrant oil running down Aaron's beard, and to dew falling on the mountains: things that run down and spread, reaching whatever they touch. Second, the honest catch. The Tao Te Ching, in chapter seventy-nine, says, in a paraphrase of James Legge's version, that when a great quarrel is settled, some resentment is sure to remain. Reconciling isn't a time machine. Two people who make up still remember. Third, what the wise one does with that. The same chapter pictures a tally, the old way of recording a debt in two halves, and says the sage keeps his half and doesn't press the other side to pay. One way to read it: reconciling isn't pretending there was no debt. It's holding the record without collecting on it. Fourth, the condition in your line. Reconciling is only a gift where it's safe. If the other person is still dangerous, still cruel, still doing the thing, the brave act may be the boundary from a few days ago, not the reunion. Nothing on this path asks anyone to walk back into harm. But where it is safe, a half-raised hand in a grocery aisle can be the start of something good and pleasant.
screen: `GOOD AND PLEASANT, TOGETHER.` · `SOME RESENTMENT REMAINS.` · `HOLD THE TALLY. DON'T COLLECT.` · `ONLY WHERE IT'S SAFE.` · then, large: `WHEN IT'S SAFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted from, where the drift is about time, pride or awkwardness, not danger. Ask yourself two questions: is it safe, and do I want this? If both answers are yes, find the simplest first sentence, short and true; if either is no, let them go back to the distance, and if you pray, you can bring them into your prayer.
Reconciling. Two people rebuilding what was broken between them: a step past forgiveness, taken only where it's safe. Today's word.
Your line: when it's safe. Where it isn't, the line is your permission to wait. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 133, and its opening Hebrew words, hinneh mah tov, are sung as a song in many Jewish communities; readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter 79 as counsel on not pressing old claims after a quarrel.

chat.says: Now that I've forgiven my old friend, do I have to be close with her again?
options: Not necessarily. Reconciling takes two, and only where it's safe and wanted.
Yes. Forgiving and reconciling are the same thing, so you're friends again.
Only if you both forget it ever happened; that's what making up means.
chat.meaning: Reconciling is a step past forgiveness, taken only where it's safe. Even then, the Tao Te Ching says some resentment remains.

notes: Tao Te Ching 79 is paraphrased from Legge (1891): a great animosity reconciled leaves a grudge remaining; the sage keeps the left-hand portion of the record of the engagement and does not insist on its fulfilment by the other party. Confirm the paraphrase and the 'tally in two halves' gloss.
